message.content:
The number of distinct legal positions that can arise in a standard game of chess is astronomically large – on the order of **10⁴³**.  

This estimate (often called the “Shannon number” after Claude Shannon) comes from counting all ways the pieces can be arranged on the board while respecting the rules (e.g., no two kings in check, pawn promotion possibilities, etc.). It’s a rough lower bound; more refined calculations put it around 10⁴³ to 10⁴⁴.

For comparison, the number of distinct possible games (sequences of moves) is even larger—roughly 10¹²³.
